red.focus: Understand why Donoghue v Stevenson recognized a duty beyond a direct contract.
red.summary: A consumer alleged illness after drinking ginger beer containing a decomposed snail, even though a friend had purchased it. The House of Lords considered whether the manufacturer could owe the consumer a duty of care.
checklist: I can identify the consumer and manufacturer in the alleged facts
I can explain why the lack of a contract mattered
I can distinguish the duty issue from proof of liability

sections.title: A consumer was not the buyer
sections.body_md: May Donoghue alleged that she became ill after drinking ginger beer from an opaque bottle that her friend had bought. The bottle allegedly contained a decomposed snail. She had no contract with the manufacturer, David Stevenson, so a simple claim founded on a sale between them was unavailable. The legal question was whether a manufacturer might nonetheless owe reasonable care to the person likely to consume its product. The House of Lords considered that issue assuming her allegations for the purpose of deciding whether her claim could proceed.
sections.audio_script: May Donoghue alleged that she became ill after drinking ginger beer from an opaque bottle that her friend had bought. The bottle allegedly contained a decomposed snail. She had no contract with the manufacturer, David Stevenson, so a simple claim founded on a sale between them was unavailable. The legal question was whether a manufacturer might nonetheless owe reasonable care to the person likely to consume its product. The House of Lords considered that issue assuming her allegations for the purpose of deciding whether her claim could proceed.

sections.title: A duty can protect foreseeable consumers
sections.body_md: In Donoghue v Stevenson (1932), the House of Lords recognized that a manufacturer might owe a duty of care to an ultimate consumer where the relevant product reached that person without reasonable opportunity for intermediate examination. Lord Atkin's neighbor principle helped explain duties toward people closely and directly affected by conduct. The judgment did not finally prove that the bottle contained a snail or that Stevenson had been negligent. It established an important possibility of legal duty beyond a direct purchase contract.

sections.title: A duty is not automatic compensation
sections.body_md: A later negligence analysis still asks whether a recognized duty existed, whether the defendant breached it, whether breach caused the alleged harm, and whether actionable loss followed. A famous case cannot substitute for those elements. Its importance is that serious harm could be legally considered even without a direct contract between consumer and manufacturer. This illustrates the social purpose of evolving private law: a person's bodily safety need not always depend on who handed money to a shopkeeper.

yellow.focus: Explain how MacPherson v Buick reduced privity barriers in product negligence.
yellow.summary: A defective automobile wheel injured a purchaser who bought through a dealer rather than directly from the manufacturer. The 1916 New York decision extended negligence duty beyond an immediate contractual purchaser.
checklist: I can describe the defective-wheel claim
I can state Cardozo's foreseeability-based duty reasoning
I can compare the timing and role of MacPherson and Donoghue

sections.title: A wheel failed after resale
sections.body_md: Donald MacPherson bought a Buick from a dealer; the car had been assembled by Buick using a wheel bought from another supplier. The wheel collapsed and caused injury. The alleged negligence included failure to inspect for a defect that a reasonable inspection could reveal. Buick argued that it owed no duty to the injured consumer because the purchaser's contract was with the dealer. The legal question concerned duty in negligence, not breach of a direct promise to the final driver.
sections.audio_script: Donald MacPherson bought a Buick from a dealer; the car had been assembled by Buick using a wheel bought from another supplier. The wheel collapsed and caused injury. The legal question concerned duty in negligence, not breach of a direct promise to the final driver.

sections.title: Cardozo reasoned beyond privity
sections.body_md: In MacPherson v Buick Motor Co. (1916), the New York Court of Appeals held that a manufacturer could owe care to foreseeable users when negligent construction of the product made danger to life and limb reasonably probable, even without contractual privity. The reasoning moved beyond narrower categories often associated with intrinsically dangerous articles. It still required a legally relevant defect, foreseeable danger, and negligent conduct. The holding was not that every manufacturer guarantees absolute safety under negligence law.
sections.audio_script: In MacPherson v Buick Motor Co. (1916), the New York Court of Appeals held that a manufacturer could owe care to foreseeable users when negligent construction of the product made danger to life and limb reasonably probable, even without contractual privity. The reasoning moved beyond narrower categories often associated with intrinsically dangerous articles. It still required a legally relevant defect, foreseeable danger, and negligent conduct. The holding was not that every manufacturer guarantees absolute safety under negligence law.

sections.title: Compare two paths to protection
sections.body_md: MacPherson preceded Donoghue by sixteen years. The cases emerged in different jurisdictions but each helped weaken the notion that only the person who directly bought a product could obtain relief for negligent manufacture. Compare the car's defective wheel with the alleged contaminated drink: in both, a third party carried the product from manufacturer to user. A careful comparison should also identify the distinct reasoning and procedural posture. Neither decision abolishes the need to prove causation or other negligence elements.

orange.focus: Analyze Fairchild v Glenhaven's limited expansion of causal responsibility.
orange.summary: A person may develop mesothelioma after asbestos exposures from multiple negligent employers, with science unable to identify which exposure caused it. Fairchild created a carefully confined approach to the causation problem.
checklist: I can explain the ordinary proof difficulty in the asbestos cases
I can identify the material-increase-in-risk approach
I can distinguish a narrow exception from universal probabilistic liability

sections.title: Several employers, one disease
sections.body_md: The workers in Fairchild v Glenhaven Funeral Services Ltd (2002) developed mesothelioma after occupational exposure to asbestos dust through different employers. Medical knowledge could not identify which particular exposure had triggered the fatal illness. Under a straightforward individual but-for test, a claimant might fail despite proof that each employer had negligently exposed the worker to the very risk of the disease. The House of Lords faced an acute conflict between ordinary causation proof and the practical impossibility of identifying the responsible fiber.
sections.audio_script: The workers in Fairchild v Glenhaven Funeral Services Ltd (2002) developed mesothelioma after occupational exposure to asbestos dust through different employers. Medical knowledge could not identify which particular exposure had triggered the fatal illness. Under a straightforward individual but-for test, a claimant might fail despite proof that each employer had negligently exposed the worker to the very risk of the disease. The House of Lords faced an acute conflict between ordinary causation proof and the practical impossibility of identifying the responsible fiber.

sections.title: The House permitted a narrow route
sections.body_md: The House of Lords allowed the claims to proceed through an approach focusing on whether an employer's breach materially increased the risk of mesothelioma in the circumstances considered. That was a significant development from ordinary causal proof. It was not a rule that any statistical correlation automatically proves every defendant caused any type of injury. The narrow factual setting and the duty intended to guard against this disease were central to the reasoning. Later legislation and cases further shaped liability and apportionment.

sections.title: Risk evidence has precise boundaries
sections.body_md: A lawyer should identify the wrongful exposure, the type of illness, scientific uncertainty, and the legal test under which increased risk is relevant. Group statistics may inform the analysis without conclusively identifying which defendant's exposure caused one person's injury. Fairchild responded to a particular evidentiary dilemma; extending it to every industrial or environmental claim would erase its limits. A strong master's-level answer defends the precise doctrinal exception rather than using fairness as a substitute for the governing rule.

black.focus: Critique expansion of tort duties and causal responsibility under industrial uncertainty.
black.summary: MacPherson and Donoghue expanded protection against negligent manufacture; Fairchild addressed a different barrier involving proof of causation. Evaluate when legal adaptation protects victims without imposing arbitrary liability.
checklist: I can distinguish enlarging duty from modifying causation
I can evaluate fairness to injured persons and defendants
I can defend principled boundaries for new technological risks

sections.title: Different legal barriers require different reforms
sections.body_md: MacPherson and Donoghue addressed the existence of duty where an injured person lacked a direct contract with a manufacturer. Fairchild addressed causation where wrongful exposures were established but the causal exposure could not be identified. Treating these as interchangeable 'pro-claimant' cases loses their doctrinal structure. In each, expanding recovery depended on specific policy and legal arguments within the jurisdiction. A doctoral lawyer should distinguish duty, breach, causation, loss, and remedy before debating whether an expansion was justified.
sections.audio_script: MacPherson and Donoghue addressed the existence of duty where an injured person lacked a direct contract with a manufacturer. Fairchild addressed causation where wrongful exposures were established but the causal exposure could not be identified. Treating these as interchangeable 'pro-claimant' cases loses their doctrinal structure. In each, expanding recovery depended on specific policy and legal arguments within the jurisdiction. A doctoral lawyer should distinguish duty, breach, causation, loss, and remedy before debating whether an expansion was justified.

sections.title: Every expansion has distributional consequences
sections.body_md: Broad duties can motivate safer product design and compensate victims, yet unlimited liability may discourage beneficial activity or unfairly burden actors who did not cause the injury. Narrow causal exceptions can address proof impossibility but may also impose liability in a particular case on someone whose conduct did not in fact trigger the illness. A defensible theory identifies which error it tolerates and why the protected activity creates a duty. It should seek evidence about deterrence, insurance, proof costs, and the experiences of people injured.

sections.title: Apply the method to an unfamiliar technology
sections.body_md: Imagine a connected medical device sold through retailers and serviced by several contractors. A patient is harmed, but the origin of the failure remains unclear. Analyze separate questions: who owed care to the end user; what duties were breached; what evidence connects breach to injury; and whether a legally recognized exceptional rule applies. Do not announce a Fairchild-style exception because causation is inconvenient. A humane doctrine protects patients while giving each accused actor a fair opportunity to dispute responsibility.
